assessmentSummary.identity: Unresolved legacy quarter-turn source. Its description says jump or bound and does not declare takeoff foot count, landing foot count or leg, displacement, turn direction, hold criterion, side accounting, or reset.
currentCardFindings: The label cannot distinguish a same-leg hop, opposite-leg bound, bilateral jump, or two-foot-to-one-foot landing.
Existing wording is not executable and cannot support its current low physical-difficulty score.
Candidate videos intentionally span bilateral and unilateral interpretations rather than resolve the source.
assessmentSummary.difficultyDecision: Do not score exercise complexity or physical difficulty until foot contracts, displacement, direction, hold, side accounting, and reset define one exercise. Athlete proficiency is excluded.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Archive as nonprescribable while preserving the source mapping and human-review decision.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Archived nonprescribable source. The source says jump or bound and does not declare takeoff foot count, landing foot count or leg, displacement, turn direction, hold criterion, side accounting, or reset.

population.reason: readiness and impact exposure cannot be matched to an undefined takeoff and landing contract

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical differences between unilateral and bilateral landings from a jump
claims: Unilateral and bilateral landings are mechanically distinct, so takeoff foot count and landing foot count are identity fields rather than synonyms.
An exact quarter-turn card must also declare rotation magnitude and direction, displacement, terminal hold, side accounting, and reset.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of unilateral and bilateral plyometric training on jumping, sprinting, and change of direction abilities
evidence.sourcePublisher: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Quarter-turn jump and hop tasks belong to plyometric jump-and-landing work, but unilateral and bilateral modes remain separate controlled identities.
The canonical family records aerial reorientation and terminal stabilization without using athlete proficiency labels.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Effects of Mid-flight Whole-Body and Trunk Rotation on Landing Mechanics: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
claims: A 90-degree whole-body reorientation and landing uses coordinated lower-limb deceleration plus pelvis and trunk control; the two legs may not share landing load equally.
Cards declare foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, trunk, and visual-orientation demands without claiming isolated muscle activation or injury prediction.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Effects of Mid-flight Whole-Body and Trunk Rotation on Landing Mechanics: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
claims: Mid-flight whole-body rotation changes landing mechanics compared with a nonrotational landing and requires control of angular momentum and reorientation before stabilization.
The authored bilateral task uses two-foot takeoff and two-foot landing; the authored unilateral task uses one declared leg for takeoff and same-leg landing.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical differences between unilateral and bilateral landings from a jump
claims: Unilateral landing changes knee motion and muscle demand compared with bilateral landing and therefore receives a higher physical-difficulty and stabilization score.

Complexity also accounts for exactly 90 degrees of aerial orientation, foot-count contract, landing alignment, hold, side completion, and reset; overall difficulty is the maximum of complexity and physical difficulty.

evidence.sourceTitle: Maximizing plyometric training for adolescents: a meta-analysis of ground contact frequency and overall intervention time on jumping ability
evidence.sourcePublisher: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Every takeoff and landing is counted in the session impact budget, with unilateral contacts tracked by side.
Contact volume, prior jumping and running exposure, surface, amplitude, landing strategy, symptoms, and recovery state must be considered before selection or progression.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: The task requires a level high-traction resilient surface, clear takeoff and landing zone, visible orientation target, safe footwear, and enough space for an uncontrolled step without collision.
Pain, instability, lower-limb restrictions, dizziness, inability to follow the stop command, or an exhausted impact budget block selection.

evidence.sourceTitle: Maximizing plyometric training for adolescents: a meta-analysis of ground contact frequency and overall intervention time on jumping ability
evidence.sourcePublisher: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Dose is stored as fully reset attempts and total landing contacts rather than a fatigue circuit or vague work interval.
The card starts with small sets, long enough rest for repeatable orientation and landing quality, and lower volume on the unilateral task.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Instruction declares start orientation, takeoff and landing foot contract, exact quarter turn, target, quiet aligned landing, hold duration, and reset before the next attempt.
Feedback is concise and externally observable; it does not promise injury prevention or prescribe a universal joint angle.

evidence.sourceTitle: Entry angle during jump landing changes biomechanical risk factors for ACL injury
claims: Landing direction changes lower-limb biomechanics, so each direction and side is screened and coached rather than assumed equivalent.
Stop for symptoms, under- or over-rotation, wrong-foot contact, audible or stiff impact, knee-foot or trunk-control loss, balance step before the hold, fatigue drift, unsafe surface, or traffic.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Plyometric Jump Training on the Reactive Strength Index in Healthy Individuals Across the Lifespan: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
claims: Quarter-turn stick landings are low-volume output or landing-control exposures performed while fresh, not sustained conditioning.
Workout generation must validate phase, impact budget, side balance, rest, surface, space, exact foot contract, and substitutions after every change.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Athlete support explains the exact foot contract, what a controlled stick looks like, expected effort, unexpected symptoms, self-checks, and how to request a lower-impact alternative.
Pain or instability is a stop signal, not a difficulty target.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Effects of Mid-flight Whole-Body and Trunk Rotation on Landing Mechanics: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
claims: Coaches observe turn magnitude, takeoff and landing feet, asymmetrical loading, trunk orientation, knee-foot alignment, landing noise, hold, symptoms, side completion, and reset.
Group delivery requires one athlete per marked zone, a shared start and stop signal, clear turn direction, and a maintained sightline.

evidence.sourceTitle: Unilateral Plyometric Jump Training Shows Significantly More Effective than Bilateral Training in Improving Both Time to Stabilization and Peak Landing Force in Single-Leg Lend and Hold Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
claims: Unilateral and bilateral options are not interchangeable accessibility labels; an easier option changes the exact exercise and requires a reviewed substitution.
Accessible delivery can reduce jump height and attempts, increase rest, use larger visual targets, and provide text, still-image, audio, or live instruction while preserving the chosen identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of Jump Direction and External Load on Single-Legged Jump-Landing Biomechanics
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Landing support, direction, displacement, external load, approach, obstacle or drop, rotation magnitude, terminal action, and reactive cue are evaluated separately.
Clockwise versus counterclockwise direction and starting side are modifiers only after takeoff, landing, displacement, rotation, and finish are fixed.
YouTube oEmbed health and embedding metadata establish current candidate availability only.

A human must watch the complete video and verify exact foot contract, 90-degree rotation, displacement, terminal hold, cueing, safety, captions, accessibility, and demonstration quality before approval.
